rows.source: HSE agriculture machinery, livestock and public safety
rows.verified: Agricultural Safe Stop means applying the handbrake, putting controls in neutral, switching off power and removing the key before leaving or intervening.

rows.source: HSE agriculture machinery, livestock and public safety
rows.verified: Safe Stop should be followed before leaving the operating position, when another person approaches and before maintenance, adjustment or blockage clearing.

rows.source: HSE agriculture machinery, livestock and public safety
rows.verified: Farm vehicles and handling equipment should be suitable, checked daily and repaired promptly when faults are found.

rows.source: HSE agriculture machinery, livestock and public safety
rows.verified: Livestock handling systems should include maintained facilities, a suitable race and crush, competent workers and controls for temperamental animals.

rows.source: HSE agriculture machinery, livestock and public safety
rows.verified: Handling cattle always presents injury risk and requires assessed, maintained and efficient handling arrangements.

rows.source: HSE agriculture machinery, livestock and public safety
rows.verified: Children under 13 must not ride on or drive agricultural self-propelled machines or certain other farm machinery.

rows.source: HSE agriculture machinery, livestock and public safety
rows.verified: Young-person risk assessments must account for inexperience, immaturity and lack of awareness of relevant hazards.

rows.source: HSE agriculture machinery, livestock and public safety
rows.verified: Farm machinery left in areas accessible to the public should be secured and left in a safe condition.

rows.source: HSE agriculture machinery, livestock and public safety
rows.verified: Agricultural controls depend on machine type, terrain, maintenance, livestock behaviour, public access, worker competence, weather and the specific operation.

rows.source: HSE agriculture machinery, livestock and public safety
rows.verified: Agricultural evidence is activity-, equipment-, animal- and site-specific and is not an exact parcel-level injury probability.

rows.source: HSE forestry and tree-work safety
rows.verified: Anyone using a chainsaw at work must receive adequate training and be competent for the particular type of chainsaw work.

rows.source: HSE forestry and tree-work safety
rows.verified: Chainsaw users must be provided with and wear appropriate PPE identified for the task and working position.

rows.source: HSE forestry and tree-work safety
rows.verified: Chainsaw PPE commonly includes suitable head, eye, hearing, hand, leg and footwear protection based on risk assessment.

rows.source: HSE forestry and tree-work safety
rows.verified: Forestry and arboriculture machinery other than chainsaws should only be used by trained and competent people.

rows.source: HSE forestry and tree-work safety
rows.verified: Tree-work training is required at induction, when risks change and when refresher or remedial training is needed.

rows.source: HSE forestry and tree-work safety
rows.verified: Tree-work training must be provided during working hours without charging employees.

rows.source: HSE forestry and tree-work safety
rows.verified: Tree work is a high-risk activity and HSE directs dutyholders to current forestry and arboriculture good-practice guidance.

rows.source: HSE forestry and tree-work safety
rows.verified: Tree work may occur near the public, highways or railways, in remote terrain and in varied weather, making effective training essential.

rows.source: HSE forestry and tree-work safety
rows.verified: Tree-work controls depend on species, tree condition, terrain, weather, public access, equipment, work position, escape routes and worker competence.

rows.source: HSE forestry and tree-work safety
rows.verified: Tree-work evidence is tree-, task-, equipment- and site-specific and is not an exact parcel-level struck-by or fall probability.
